newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: S.African farm project in Mozambique set to start.
newsitem.headline: S.African farm project in Mozambique set to start.

text.p: White South African farmers will start agricultural and livestock production in Mozambique next month, a senior Mozambican official said on Wednesday.
But predictions that large numbers of Afrikaners would quickly occupy northern Niassa province under the Mosagrius scheme have not materialised.

The chairman of the Mosagrius management board, Antonio Muacorica, told the Maputo daily Noticias newspaper that only 14 South African farmers were actually in Niassa, with 30 others ready to join in.
The Mosagrius Corporation is owned by the Mozambican and South African governments, and it is under its auspices that South African farmers are to settle in Niassa.

Contacts are under way with international organisations and financial institutions to raise funds to finance those farmers who have expressed an interest in taking part in the programme but do not have enough money of their own.
Muacorica said about 200 Mozambicam farmers have been enrolled for the joint venture.
He also said the Mozambican government had decided to exempt the South African farmers participating in Mosagrius from customs duties on agricultural and other equipment to be used in the programme.
Mosagrius has been granted a total of 220,000 hectares, of which 100,000 is in the district of Majune in the Lugenda valley and is intended for growing crops.
A further 100,000 hectares in Sanga is for livestock, and the remaining 20,000 hectares is intended for eco-tourism in areas still to be defined.

Fertile but sparsely populated, Niassa province is the first part of the "promised land" being made available for the new trekkers, who are expected to bring skills and investment to aid-dependent Mozambique.
President Nelson Mandela signed the authorisation for the farmers' move with Mozambican leader Joaquim Chissano last year.

The relocation has been billed as a repeat of the Great Trek north from the Cape by Afrikaners which started in 1835. Participants in that migration, seeking to escape British colonialist rule, eventually dominated what is now South Africa.
